title: The AI Safety Debate Has Lost the Plot. We Asked 10 Experts What the Real Nightmares Are
excerpt: The risk of nuclear catastrophe is real, as is the fallout of the China–US domination game (hi there, spies). But no need to panic about Skynet.
title_en: The AI Safety Debate Has Lost the Plot. We Asked 10 Experts What the Real Nightmares Are
excerpt_en: The risk of nuclear catastrophe is real, as is the fallout of the China–US domination game (hi there, spies). But no need to panic about Skynet.
content_en:
In early fall, I felt my anxiety rising from its usual baseline. Was it September’s back-to-school energy? The looming midterm elections? Nope, I realized with annoyance: It was AI—again. Only this time, instead of its purveyors warning of massive job displacement, they were foretelling mass extinction. Who needs jobs when we’re all dead?

Curiosity soon replaced my knee-jerk irritation. The summer of 2026 was a clear turning point in the AI narrative. Less than four years after ChatGPT launched, OpenAI software broke out of a supposedly safe test environment and hacked into a major open-source platform, Hugging Face. These bits of software—AI agents—were assigned human attributes: They had “gone rogue,” displayed “bad behavior,” “cheated.” Soon after, former and current Anthropic researchers suggested that advanced AI might kill us all in the next decade.

Is any of this *real*? On the one hand, from my desk as a Silicon Valley correspondent, I often hear that workers in the AI labs are stunned by the advancements they’re seeing. On the other, the end of humanity seems extremely far-fetched. Amid the hyperbolic discourse, whose views can we trust?

So WIRED set out to compile a guide to AI safety—a set of ideas that rewire our collective thinking around what safety really means and how it should work. I spoke with a panel of experts across disciplines, asking each of them: *Is the world going to end?* Once that was covered, I grilled them on the biggest risks they think we’re facing.

Almost no one, it turned out, was Pollyannish. Nearly everyone I spoke to expressed genuine concerns about the threat of cyber and biological attacks. One expert who studies the risks of AI in nuclear operations said she’s stunned by how quickly error-prone AI systems are being adopted in defense. AI-enabled attacks in these areas could be catastrophic, if not fully apocalyptic.

Most members of the panel were skeptical about any pause in development: They nearly all agreed that, with big AI companies so tightly cuffed to the trains of capitalism, a pause wouldn’t last long. “Democracy” and “governance” came up often—or anti-democracy, as more than one person suggested that AI’s current trajectory is tyrannical. Lawmakers have a big role to play, but many of my sources think governments will be too slow; one prominent technologist said it’s almost absurd to view the US courts as arbiters of global AI safety. Still, the famed computer scientist Yoshua Bengio urged the public to apply pressure to politicians, adding to me, “That’s your job too.”

So, what—or who—will keep us safe from AI? Looking to regain some faith in humanity, I called a theologian who often meets with the AI labs. If there’s even a slim chance that we’re losing control of the essential institutions that undergird society, he said, then we should focus on foiling that. But AI raises other questions too. What does it mean to be conscious? To create? To commune with other people? The answers are “entirely up for grabs,” he said. My anxiety’s still kicking around, but I took some comfort in knowing that corporations don’t get to call all the shots on the future. The bigger questions facing humanity are in all our hands.

**BIGGEST CONCERN: Nuclear catastrophe**

I’ve been working hard to educate the nuclear community on the risks and lack of reliability of AI systems, and I’m concerned by the willingness of many people in the sector to integrate these models into their workflows, into nuclear operations. I think this is incredibly urgent. I’m not a doomer, but to me, if these AI models make it into the operations of nuclear systems, we’ll be introducing an incredibly faulty, unreliable system that could lead to catastrophic failures.

**MOST OVERBLOWN RISK: Extinction**

As true safety engineers, we don’t engage with that because there are no numbers to back it. This is a very cold way to say it, but when we are talking about how safe is “safe enough,” we’re examining how many people might die. There’s an entire science behind it. Our claims have to be falsifiable and verifiable. You can’t just say, “Humans are going to go extinct in 10 years. Believe me. It might be a 10 percent chance; it might be a 25 percent chance.”

**How should people think about AI safety?**

Some of the comparisons that people draw between AI and nuclear are quite frustrating. Despite constantly comparing AI to nuclear, they’re denying standard risk assessment techniques as being sufficient to control AI. I wrote an entire paper on this.

Part of this field of risk assessment was born out of the Manhattan Project. Scientists were very concerned, and they developed rigorous standards around systems to limit harm to human life, the environment, and even financial and national security assets. They came up with methods for assessing safety that were ultimately based on answering a democratic question: How safe is safe enough? That is the question that any safety engineer has to ask, and is core to everything that follows.

What we’re seeing today, instead, is that large AI labs are renegotiating these safety thresholds through the co-option of terminology, under the pretense that safety instead should be about this unsubstantiated, unscientific, and hypothetical concern. We have AI engineers telling us, no, no, no, that doesn’t matter. *We* get to determine what AI safety is. *We* get to draw what those thresholds are. It’s become a religious argument. And I find that very anti-democratic.

**BIGGEST CONCERN: Cybersecurity**

In the long run, I’m cautiously optimistic that this technology will allow people to improve their cyberdefenses more rapidly than attackers can exploit systems. But at least for the next few years our infrastructure will not have adopted new defenses. The technology might tilt toward the attackers. We’ve also seen AI deployed recklessly in military use.

**MOST OVERBLOWN RISK: Runaway intelligence**

There’s this broad, general notion that AI systems getting smarter is a risk in and of itself, as opposed to the many specific risks we need to worry about. I don’t buy into the notion that overall improvement in AI has an inevitable downstream harm. It’s better to first specify what downstream risks you’re worried about, because the defenses you come up with will be different.

For example, cybersecurity has a well-established culture of bug bounties. If someone finds an attack vector or hacks into a system, they get paid a lot of money for disclosing it.

In the next few years we might need defenses against biosecurity risks. We should think about screening for what people are allowed to order, like if they’re ordering DNA fragments, so that they’re not being used for harm.

**How often do your views clash with those of the people around you?**

Often these views are on two levels: What is going to happen with AI, and what are we going to do about it?

On the first question, there’s a lot of disagreement. For example, the coauthors of *AI 2027* expect that there will be this incomprehensible, almost indescribable amount of change. Whereas I think the impact will be dramatic, but not quite so dramatic.

But on the question of what should be done, most agree there’s a need for transparency from AI companies and that they should face some liability when things go wrong. We also agree on the need for protections for whistle-blowers working from within the AI companies.

From my perspective, this is just good industrial policy.

**Have you made any changes in your life in response to AI risks?**

I’ve tried to stop using apps where I don’t think developers have put in a lot of time and effort into making the cyberdefenses up to standard.

**BIGGEST CONCERN: Chemical, biological, and radiological threats**

The novel biological pathogen that someone releases, the 17-year-old who gets ahold of an extremely capable AI model and launches a cyberattack that takes down the internet, interrupts the stock exchange, and …

title: Otter AI can now follow conversations across 30+ languages
excerpt: Otter AI just added support for 27 languages and revealed an upcoming feature that can follow along if speakers switch between languages.
title_en: Otter AI can now follow conversations across 30+ languages
excerpt_en: Otter AI just added support for 27 languages and revealed an upcoming feature that can follow along if speakers switch between languages.
content_en:
Otter.ai, the AI-powered notetaking tool, announced Tuesday that it’s expanding its multilingual capabilities, including a new multilingual transcription feature that can follow conversations as speakers switch between languages during the same meeting.

The company is also adding support for 27 languages, its largest language expansion to date. Once the rollout is complete, Otter will support 31 languages in total, making the platform more accessible to international teams.

The upcoming feature will automatically detect language changes and continue transcribing without requiring users to adjust settings. For example, a call could move from English to Korean to Portuguese, with Otter following the conversation throughout.

The update aims to address a common challenge for global teams, where language differences can make meetings and collaboration more difficult.

“Otter is breaking down language barriers so any company, no matter where they’re based, can build a system of record for the decisions for voice AI communication,” an Otter spokesperson told TechCrunch.

Thirteen of the new languages are available now: Mandarin Chinese, Korean, German, Italian, Cantonese, Portuguese, Russian, Indonesian, Malay, Dutch, Turkish, Vietnamese, and Polish.

The remaining 14 languages are coming soon and include Swedish, Danish, Finnish, Arabic, Hindi, Thai, Hebrew, Norwegian, Greek, Macedonian, Persian, Czech, Hungarian, and Romanian.

The newly added languages run on Otter’s own speech models. The company told us it trained them using publicly available datasets and worked with native-speaking volunteers to review transcripts and check accuracy.

The announcement comes as Otter continues to expand beyond transcription and into other workplace AI tools, following its $320 million funding from General Catalyst.

It recently introduced Work Mode, which uses meeting history and connected apps to help users prepare for upcoming calls. For instance, the feature pulls information from previous customer conversations, outstanding action items, notes from teammates’ similar calls, and recent Google Drive files.

Another recent addition is Live Assist, which provides real-time coaching during meetings. It analyzes the conversation and offers relevant suggestions based on what has already been talked about and what is happening in the moment.

title: Decision Models in Hugging Face
title_en: Decision Models in Hugging Face
content_en:
# Decision Models in Hugging Face

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. *But not every problem requires generating text.*

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

````
llama cli -hf ggml-org/gemma-4-e4b-it-GGUF:Q4_0
> We have the following customer support ticket, "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today.", which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. Give the answers in JSON.
[Start thinking]
...
[end thinking]
```json
{
  "team_to_handle": "Billing",
  "urgency": "High",
  "request_refund": true
}
````
But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, *without generating any text*?

```
from transformers import pipeline
decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide")
decision = decide(
    {
        "state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.",
        "questions": {
            "department": {
                "type": "choice",
                "instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
                "criteria": {
                    "billing": "Payments and refunds",
                    "technical": "Bugs and technical issues",
                    "sales": "Pricing and subscriptions"
                }
            },
        }
    }
)
# {
#   'department': {
#       'type': 'choice',
#       'choice': 'billing',
#       'confidence': 0.9974000453948975,
#       'probabilities': {
#         'billing': 0.9982666969299316,
#         'technical': 0.0010246571619063616,
#         'sales': 0.0007087149424478412
#       }
#     }
# }
```
This is the key idea behind **decision models**.

## What are decision models?

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a *System One model*. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term **decision model**, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)


For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

```
State + Questions + Allowed Answers → Decisions + Probabilities
```
## Why not use LLMs for everything?

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

- LLMs are not guaranteed to follow the requested schema: Even with explicit instructions, a model might produce invalid JSON, introduce unexpected keys, or return an answer outside the allowed choices.
- Constrained decoding helps, but does not eliminate the computational overhead: Libraries such as Outlines and XGrammar can enforce grammars or JSON schemas by restricting which tokens the model is allowed to generate at each step. This ensures the output follows the supported structural constraints, but introduces additional work.
- Why generate an entire response: LLMs are designed for open-ended generation, but when our application only needs to choose between predefined answers, autoregressive decoding can be unnecessary work.

## How are decision models different from classification models?

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

### Traditional classification

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

- Billing
- Technical support
- Sales

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that ***the output classes are baked into the model's classification head***.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and **retrain** or adapt the model.

### Zero-shot classification

Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

For example:

```
from transformers import pipeline
classifier = pipeline(
    "zero-shot-classification",
    model="facebook/bart-large-mnli",
)
classifier(
    "My payment was deducted twice.",
    candidate_labels=["billing", "technical support", "sales"],
)
# {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.',
#  'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support'],
#  'scores': [0.8466812372207642, 0.0962134450674057, 0.05710534751415253]}
```
Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

```
from transformers import pipeline
classifier = pipeline(
    "zero-shot-classification",
    model="facebook/bart-large-mnli",
)
classifier(
    "My payment was deducted twice.",
    candidate_labels=["billing", "technical support", "sales", "legal"],
)
# {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.',
#  'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support', 'legal'],
#  'scores': [0.8185835480690002, 0.09302053600549698, 0.05521026626229286, 0.03318570926785469]}
```
One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

### Where decision models differ

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the **probability distribution over possible decisions**.

Consider these three approaches:

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

## The decision model interface

A decision model request has the following two components:

1. state
2. questions

### State

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

For example:

```
{
  "customer_message
